News.title: Scientists 'stunned' by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
News.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.

News.title: Two jailed for violent disorder at asylum hotel
News.content:
Two men have been jailed for more than two years after taking part in protests outside an asylum hotel in Essex last summer.

An "aggressive mob" of hundreds of people gathered outside the Bell Hotel in Epping, Essex, in July 2025, after one of the migrants living there was charged with sexual assault, Chelmsford Crown Court heard.

Jonathan Glover, 47, from Springfields, Waltham Abbey, was sentenced to two years and six months in prison for violent disorder.

Charlie Land, 24, from Warren Close in Hatfield, Hertfordshire, sobbed as he received a two year and eight month sentence for violent disorder and criminal damage.

The pair were found guilty at Chelmsford Crown Court following a trial in June.

News.title: Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise
News.content:
Competition for degree apprenticeships in England has quadrupled over the past three years, the BBC has found.

The popularity of degree apprenticeships - which offer a paid-for university degree along with a salary - has grown as the cost of university has come under increased scrutiny.

Data seen by the BBC showed the number of applicants through the government's central platform nearly tripled from 8,100 to 21,800 over the past three years, while the number of positions available fell by almost half, from 7,300 to 3,700.

Applicants said they applied to university as a "backup" because competition was so fierce, with employers cutting back on hiring because of high employment costs and economic uncertainty.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it was "backing employers who take on young apprentices".

Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure teenagers had technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to stay at home home rather than moving away, to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments. The cost of undergraduate tuition fees in England is now set to rise every year with inflation.

Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.

News.title: 'Missing' Baptiste serving prison sentence in Morocco
News.content:
An English athletics coach and former gold medallist said by media reports to be missing was given a 10-month prison sentence in Morocco for sexually assaulting a minor, BBC Sport can reveal.

Leon Baptiste, who was coaching a clutch of top British track athletes in the run-up to this summer's Commonwealth Games and European Championships, suddenly went off the grid more than three months ago.

Neither UK Athletics, for whom he worked as a consultant sprinting coach, nor the sprinters he coached knew why he was out of contact.

In May, Baptiste sent the group of athletes he coached a short message saying he would be absent from training "for a while". They have been given no further explanation.

Over the weekend, he was reported in the media as being "missing" and was said to have disappeared in Morocco.

On Tuesday, a brief email was sent to the people coached on behalf of Baptiste - the 200m gold medallist at the 2010 Commonwealth Games - in which he resigned from the position, citing unspecified ill health.

A source at the Moroccan Ministry of Justice confirmed to BBC Sport that Baptiste was arrested in Marrakech in May, has subsequently been convicted and is now serving a custodial sentence in Al-Oudaya prison.

"In relation to the reports concerning the alleged 'disappearance of Leon Baptiste' - an English athletics coach reportedly missing in Morocco for more than two months under questionable circumstances - please note that the information published in this regard is inaccurate and does not reflect the facts of the case," said the source.

"The foreign national concerned had not lost contact with his surroundings and was not subject to any disappearance or unexplained absence.

"He is currently being held at the local prison in Marrakech, where he is serving a custodial sentence following his conviction by the competent judicial authorities in connection with a misdemeanour case."

They added Baptiste, 41, was "in good health".

A spokesperson for the Morocco Public Prosecution Office confirmed the sentence and nature of the conviction, adding: "The British national is currently being held at the local prison in Marrakech, where he is serving a custodial sentence following a court judgment against him in connection with his involvement in a criminal case."

In Morocco, a minor is deemed to be under 18.

Asked directly about Baptiste, a UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are supporting a British national who is detained in Morocco and are in contact with the authorities."

Sources told BBC Sport that Baptiste travelled to Marrakech with three other British former athletes, who have all since returned to the UK.

BBC Sport has made attempts to contact the athletes but had no reply.

Baptiste's family are understood to be aware of his imprisonment.

News.title: First giant tuna caught off Yorkshire since 1960s
News.content:
An Atlantic bluefin tuna has been caught and brought to shore on the Yorkshire coast for the first time in an estimated 60 years.

The giant fish had not been landed in the North Sea since the 1960s due to overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals, according to researchers from the University of Exeter who have now tagged six off Whitby.

On Sunday, the five-person crew on board The Dominator landed a whopping 338kg specimen before repeating the feat a day later with a fish that weighed "just a little bit" less, according to crew member Jack Gardner.

"I have never caught anything like it," said the 28-year-old from the village of Paull, near Hull, describing it as the "best feeling ever".

Gardner, who has been on board The Dominator since 2018, said the crew had been about 10 miles (16km) from Whitby Harbour on Sunday when they made their first catch.

"It jumped out of the water, we all just looked at each other in awe," he said.

"We couldn't believe that we had actually hooked into one."

News.title: Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School investigated over 'drip pricing'
News.content:
Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School are being investigated by the consumer watchdog over concerns they are not showing full prices upfront to customers.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is examining whether the three companies engaged in so-called 'drip pricing', which is an illegal practice where mandatory fees are not included in the headline price shown to customers.

If the CMA concludes that the firms have broken the law, it can fine them or order them to compensate customers.

The three companies said they were committed to transparency for customers and would engage fully with the CMA.

In the case of Trainline, the CMA said it observed fees of up to Â£2.79 being added on to headline train fares, and up to Â£1.50 for coach bookings.

"Both are costs that can add up for frequent travellers," the CMA said.

Trainline has been accused of drip pricing before. In 2023, the Office of Rail and Road said it and six other third-party train ticket sellers were not being upfront about fees.

Virgin Atlantic is being investigated to see whether mandatory resort fees and local taxes were included in the upfront prices shown to customers buying package holidays. The CMA said these fees vary but can go up to hundreds of pounds, significantly increasing the cost of a holiday.

And the watchdog is looking into whether RED Driving School included mandatory booking fees and digital fees in the upfront price shown to people buying driving lessons. The CMA said the fees could be more than Â£7 per lesson.

Earlier this year, the CMA ordered two other driving schools to give refunds to more than 80,000 customers after they did not disclose the total price for lessons upfront during the online booking process.

Emma Cochrane, the CMA's executive director for consumer protection, said: "The first price customers see should be the price they pay.

"At a time when many households are watching every pound they spend, it is important that people are not surprised by extra fees when booking train and coach tickets, holidays or driving lessons."

A spokesperson for Virgin Atlantic Holidays said it takes its responsibility to customers "incredibly seriously", adding: "we always want to ensure they can make an informed decision when booking a holiday with us.

"Mandatory fees are indicated at multiple stages throughout the booking journey. We are reviewing the points raised by the CMA carefully and will cooperate fully with its investigation."

A Trainline spokesperson said the company was "committed to offering customers a transparent booking experience with clear pricing and genuine value.

"We've proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and we are taking proactive steps to enhance how certain fees are presented to our customers."

Red Driving School said it was disappointed at being included in a wider investigation.

"Red Driver Training always values both transparency and consumer satisfaction in all of our interactions with our customers," a spokesperson said.

"We take any and all of our obligations under consumer law with utmost focus and seriousness."

Since last year, the CMA has had the power to rule that consumer laws have been broken without having to take businesses to court.

Consumer rights group Which? said the CMA should not hesitate to use these powers, "especially after each firm has already received a warning advisory letter".

Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, said: "Following comments made by the Prime Minister last week that unfair pricing practices have no place in our economy, this move sends a clear message to other businesses to follow the rules.

"At a time when household budgets are under strain, consumers must have confidence that businesses aren't there to rip them off and that the regulator is willing to step in to protect their rights."

News.title: Why has Russia threatened the UK and what happens next?
News.content:
Russia has warned of "consequences" following confirmation that British-made drones were used in recent Ukrainian strikes in Russia.

The Russian embassy in the UK accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis" as Kyiv has stepped up attacks on Moscow and other parts of the country in recent weeks.

In particular, the attacks have targeted oil refineries and warehouses of the largest online retailer Wildberries.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said London will continue "to support Ukraine 100%".

The BBC's Caroline Hawley explains what we know about Russia's warning.

More on this story.

News.title: Personal bankruptcy filings are surging as Americans struggle with debt. Here’s what I did to avoid one
News.content:

The number of Americans who file for bankruptcy is growing. More than 500,000 people took this step in 2025, nearly 50% more than in 2022. And the numbers have kept on climbing, with a 12% jump in June 2026 from a year earlier as many consumers struggled to pay their bills.

I am a business school professor who has researched bankruptcies and whether, when you are at the end of your financial rope, bankruptcy helps or hurts.

I became interested in the subject while in graduate school. Not because of any courses I took, but because I ran out of money. While I was in grad school, my wife, who was keeping the family afloat, unexpectedly lost her job at the very moment our savings went to zero.

Ultimately, we didn’t declare bankruptcy, and I’ll explain later what we did to avoid it. But this near brush with that fate sparked my long-term interest in this predicament that befalls many American consumers who find themselves financially stressed out.

open image in gallery The number of Americans who file for bankruptcy is growing ( Getty Images )

What’s personal bankruptcy?

Bankruptcy is a legal process for people who can’t pay their debts. Because it usually requires liquidating their assets or entering a repayment plan, Americans generally turn to it as a last resort. To declare bankruptcy you first file a petition with a federal court, which appoints a trustee to oversee your case.

But bankruptcy does not discharge all debts.

There are 19 types of debts that even bankruptcy will not wipe out. Some of the bigger categories are alimony, child support and most taxes. Student loans can be wiped out, but getting that done is difficult and it’s not an automatic part of bankruptcy proceedings.

2 conflicting goals

U.S. bankruptcy law has two big goals that contradict each other.

The first is to give honest individual debtors a “fresh start.” The process ideally reduces or eliminates enough of their debt to make it possible to earn, spend, borrow and repay money like people with a more typical financial life. In other words, personal bankruptcy can take the financial noose off debtors’ necks.

The second is to ensure that creditors get repaid as much as possible for their loans. When someone declares bankruptcy, some or maybe all of their creditors don’t get their money back. In 2024, the Americans who filed for bankruptcy had about US$75 billion in assets, but they owed their creditors about $86 billion – $11 billion more.

States and the federal government make different trade-offs between these goals. As a result there are very different limits on how much equity – the difference between market value and what you owe – debtors can keep in their primary homes and personal property after they declare bankruptcy.

Some states are quite lenient. For example, Texas bankruptcy law doesn’t limit the amount of equity in a home at all. That helps debtors get back on their feet.

Other states are extremely strict in this regard. Arkansas limits home equity after personal bankruptcy to $800, and Kentucky restricts it to $5,000. This helps creditors: Lenders can force a debtor’s house to be sold and keep much of the equity the debtor built up.

Likewise, laws protecting vehicles and other kinds of personal property belonging to people who declare bankruptcy vary widely.

2 types of personal bankruptcy

People declaring bankruptcy typically file using either Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 of the federal bankruptcy code.

About 2 in 3 people use Chapter 7, a form of financial liquidation. The bankruptcy court appoints a trustee, who then sells off all of a person’s possessions, except what is covered by the various exemptions.

The trustee then gives creditors whatever money is left after the sale. In exchange for giving up most of what someone owns, filing Chapter 7 wipes out almost all debts and gives them a fresh financial start.

For people earning moderate to high incomes and whose debts are less than $2.75 million, bankruptcy courts make them use Chapter 13.

Chapter 13 is a slower-moving process. Creditors are paid over three to five years from a person’s earnings. Debtors keep enough of their wages to cover necessary living expenses, but all other disposable income goes to creditors. Chapter 13 allows people to save their homes from foreclosure and keep their vehicles.

Bankruptcy filing rising after decline

The number of personal bankruptcies filed annually fell sharply for more than a decade before the recent uptick, hitting a low of about 368,000 in 2022, down from about 1.5 million in 2010.

That number has climbed steadily since 2022.

A 2005 law called the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act sparked the earlier decline. Its goal was to make declaring bankruptcy harder and more expensive. Many creditors pushed for these changes because they felt some individuals were abusing the system.

The changes introduced income limits for eligibility to declare Chapter 7 bankruptcy. It also required people to get credit counseling before filing to see whether there was any way they could avoid bankruptcy. It also added a new obligation: Americans now take a course in financial management after they file for bankruptcy to reduce the chance of future money troubles.

One interesting study regarding the legislation’s impact found that it lowered credit card interest rates, but it also prevented some people without health insurance from wiping out their medical debts.

The 2005 changes caused the number of personal bankruptcies to plunge. That ended with the Great Recession, which lasted from late 2007 until mid-2009.

This economic downturn pushed up the number of bankruptcies dramatically. But then the number fell from 2010 until 2022, as the Great Recession’s impact gradually receded. The decline continued into the early 2020s because the stimulus checks and more generous unemployment insurance payments the government provided at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic helped keep millions of U.S. consumers afloat.

The numbers began to rise again in 2022 as American consumers began facing increasing stress from income that has not kept pace with inflation and a sharp jump in credit card interest rates.

Lasting changes

Bankruptcy stays on your credit report for up to 10 years. After that, creditors are supposed to treat people who filed for it like anyone else. A study I worked on with law professor Lois Lupica tracked what happened over two decades to both people who had and had not declared bankruptcy. We wanted to see whether those who had filed for bankruptcy really got out of their financial hole.

Our findings were a good news, bad news story. The good news was that bankruptcy was not causing permanent financial stigma. The average person who declared bankruptcy eventually caught up financially with their peers who hadn’t.

The bad news was that it took 15-25 years to recover in almost all financial dimensions. This is longer than those 10 years that the bankruptcy filing stays on your credit report.

In short, we determined that bankruptcy does give people a fresh start, but getting that reprieve takes longer than the law’s intent.

About the author Jay L. Zagorsky is an Associate Professor of Business, Boston University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Strategies that can stave off bankruptcy

My wife and I avoided bankruptcy primarily by doing two things.

First, we switched to using cash for most of our day-to-day purchases. When our wallets were empty, we were done spending. I talk more about this in my 2025 book “The Power of Cash.”

Second, we contacted the financial company where we owed our biggest monthly payment. After providing proof of financial hardship, they were surprisingly flexible.

If these two steps are not enough for you, the next step is to consult an attorney who specializes in bankruptcy law. While there are lots of things most people can competently do on their own, filing for bankruptcy is not one of them.

News.content:

Ukraine’s corruption crisis continues to deepen, with President Volodymyr Zelensky forced to fire one of his most senior officials after they were suspected of money-laundering.

Iryna Mudra was sacked on Wednesday, the day after recently-fired defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov put further pressure on the Ukrainian leader by calling for national elections.

While Kyiv has seized the initiative in its war with Russia with an ongoing long-range drone strike campaign, Zelensky continues to be beset by domestic political challenges.

Corruption investigators have not given much away about the ongoing probe, which is working to expose a criminal organization allegedly involving senior officials from the presidential office and others.

open image in gallery Mykhailo Fedorov (L) and Zelensky had been close allies since 2019 until the former was fired ( AFP/Getty )

They stand accused of having laundered 150 million hryvnias (£2.5 million) to pay bail for a defendant in a major graft case last year, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau said.

Zelensky’s political resilience has been tested several times in the past year. His former chief of staff was charged with corruption and money laundering in May as Ukraine’s galvanised watchdog pressed on with its widening investigation.

The Independent looks at the implications of the ongoing inquiries into alleged Ukrainian corruption.

What are the latest allegations to rock Ukraine?

The latest suspects in the corruption case include a former lawmaker, the chairperson of a state bank’s board and the head of the bank’s supervisory board, the bureau said.

It also involves a deputy head of the presidential office, it added.

Zelensky, who has not been personally implicated, has not made any public comment on the investigation. But on Wednesday, he issued a decree dismissing Mudra - who has not been named by investigators - as the deputy head of the Office of the President.

Mudra’s office was searched on Wednesday, lawmaker Oleksii Honcharenko said according to The Associated Press.

A source told The Kyiv Independent that the offices member of parliament Vadym Stolar and Maksym Mykytas, a former member of parliament, were also being searched during the probe.

Stolar said in a post on Facebook: “I can confirm that the NABU is conducting investigative actions at my home. I am fully cooperating with the bureau and am not obstructing the work of law enforcement in any way."

Officials from Sense Bank that are under investigation are allegedly CEO Oleksiy Stupak and Mykola Hladyshchenko, the outlet reported.

The Yermak case

open image in gallery Andriy Yermak, previously one of the president’s closest advisors, is accused of laundering millions ( Reuters )

Zelensky has been dogged by high-level graft investigations into some of his closest allies.

Andriy Yermak, who was until late last year the president’s closest advisor, was accused of laundering some UAH 460 million (£7.73m) through luxury accommodation near Kyiv. He denies ownership in the project.

Ukraine’s top anti-corruption agencies announced today they had charged six suspects in connection to the probe, which they said was linked to Operation Midas, the growing crackdown on an alleged plot to skim $100m from the country’s energy sector.

The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAP) alleged the suspects were part of an organised group laundering assets they had obtained illegally.

A law enforcement source told the Kyiv Independent that Timur Mindich, a close associate of Zelensky, and former deputy prime minister Oleksiy Chenyshov were also among those newly charged.

The head of the bureau, buoyed in recent years to investigate allegations of graft in the top tiers of government, said on Tuesday that Zelensky was not currently a subject of any such probe.

open image in gallery Zelensky and Yermak in Kyiv in 2024 ( Reuters )

They say the money was laundered over a period of four years, from 2021 to 2025, through the cottage complex in Kozyn, a settlement of 3,500 people just south of Kyiv.

A source told the Kyiv Independent that suspects in that case allegedly gave money to Chernyshov, the former deputy PM, for the construction of the homes in Kozyn.

One of the houses said to have been financed through the Energoatom scheme was meant for Yermak, the source said.

What is Operation Midas?

The watchdogs said Yermak’s charges relate to Midas, an investigation into an alleged $100m (£74m) corruption scandal surrounding Energoatom, a public energy company and the largest producer of electricity in Ukraine.

Anti-corruption investigators announced Operation Midas in November, saying their discovery was the result of 15 months of wiretapping work and cited 1,000 hours of audio recordings and more than 70 raids.

At the heart of the probe was $100 million in funds that NABU said had been laundered by an alleged criminal organisation consisting of current and former energy officials, government ministers, a former deputy prime minister, and a businessman.

open image in gallery Former Energy Minister Herman Galushchenko (C) leaves after a court hearing over his detention ( AFP/Getty )

The accused are said to have manipulated contracts at Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear energy company, to take kickbacks - secret payments in exchange for favours.

NABU said the group took bribes from contractors worth some 10-15 per cent of each contract’s value.

Crucially, some of these contracts were handed out to build up fortifications against Russian attacks on energy infrastructure.

The scandal emerged as Ukraine battled rolling blackouts as Russia pounded energy infrastructure through a particularly bleak winter.

Who has been affected?

Investigators claim to have traced the scheme to Timur Mindich, a film producer and co-owner of President Zelensky’s former TV studio, Kvartal95.

The two were close until at least 2021, when Mindich held a surprise party for Zelensky at his flat, during the lockdowns.

Mindich fled Ukraine in the night of 10 November 2025, just hours before NABU enforcers raided his home.

Prosecutors also claimed that Rustem Umerov, a former defence minister, was pressured to buy cheaply made Chinese bulletproof vests at extortionate rates.

open image in gallery Protesters gather to oppose a law removing the independent of NABU and SAP, in Kyiv last July ( AFP/Getty )

He has not been charged and has denied wrongdoing, saying the contract was terminated due to the product’s failure to meet requirements.

Umerov remains heavily involved in Ukraine’s dialogues with the United States aimed at ending the war with Russia.

German Galushchenko, who led the energy department from 2021 until 2025, was detained by border guards in February as he tried to leave the country on a train, officials said.

Investigators said the charges were related to an alleged scheme involving offshore companies benefiting his relatives. Galushchenko - also known as Herman Halushchenko - has denied wrongdoing.

How widespread is corruption in Ukraine?

Ukraine inherited a legacy of corruption when it gained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Despite the considerable strides of NABU and SAPO since 2015, corruption remains endemic.

Today, 87 per cent of Ukrainians perceive corruption as a widespread phenomenon, according to a survey of more than 1,000 respondents last summer.

This is more sharply felt in rural communities. But only seven per cent of respondents believe corruption has improved as a whole since last year.

Last year, Transparency International - an organisation monitoring corruption around the world - gave Ukraine a score of 36 out of 100 in the Corruption Perceptions Index, with a lower score reflecting higher rates of corruption.

The UK, by comparison, received a score of 70 in 2025, reflecting a steady backslide from 82 over the last decade.

Andrii Borovyk, executive director at Transparency International Ukraine, said that despite limited improvements - such as a push for greater transparency on the handling of seized assets - reforms have been overshadowed by efforts to limit the independence of the anti-corruption agencies, until they collapsed under public and international pressure.

Ukraine saw the first major protests in the streets since the 2022 invasion in July after Zelensky suggested reining NABU and SAPO in to “cleanse” them of what he called “Russian influence”.

The EU has said deep-seated corruption is one of the major hurdles for the membership in the economic bloc Ukraine keenly desires.

News.title: Inscription on bullet shows Charlie Kirk was targeted for his politics, prosecutors say
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Prosecutors in Charlie Kirk's killing say the inscription “Hey Facist! CATCH!” on an engraved bullet shows that Kirk was targeted for how the defendant perceived his politics.

Whether defendant Tyler Robinson acted out of political animus could be key for prosecutors seeking the death penalty, or for his attorneys in taking that punishment off the table.

The prosecution and defense have filed dueling documents focused on whether the crime included aggravating factors that would make Robinson eligible for the death penalty if he’s convicted at trial. Those include political targeting and whether the shooting endangered thousands of others who attended Kirk's Sept. 10 event at Utah Valley University.

Robinson is charged with crimes including aggravated murder and has not yet entered a plea. The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting.

During a July hearing, investigators presented DNA analyses that they said linked Robinson to both the suspected murder weapon and a tool he allegedly used to engrave the bullet cartridges ( Reuters )

The latest batch of court documents follows a five-day preliminary hearing in July, when prosecutors presented what they said was “overwhelming” evidence against Robinson, while defense attorneys worked to sow doubt about analysts’ findings.

Judge Tony Graf said he will decide if the case should advance to trial after he hears again from both sides on Sept. 1.

In a document filed late Tuesday, prosecutors argued the engraved bullet found in the suspected murder weapon was an “overt political reference." They also noted that Robinson allegedly wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out."

Robinson's attorneys have argued that the text message is not strong enough evidence to prove a political motivation. They did not immediately respond to a request for comment on prosecutors' new filing.

Before his death, Kirk and the organization he co-founded, Turning Point USA, galvanized the conservative youth vote to help President Donald Trump win a second term.

Prosecutors contend that Kirk’s opposition to same-sex marriage and gender-affirming care stood in sharp contrast to Robinson, who was reportedly in a romantic relationship with his roommate, Lance Twiggs. Twiggs told investigators he had considered a gender transition around the time of Kirk's killing, according to prosecutors.

A handwritten note that prosecutors allege Robinson left for Twiggs read in part, “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it.”

In a recorded interview shown in court last month, Twiggs said he had never heard Robinson talk about Kirk before the shooting. Robinson also did not talk much about gender issues or LGBTQ+ rights, but he did sometimes talk about politics, including Trump, Twiggs told investigators.

During the July hearing, investigators presented DNA analyses that they said linked Robinson to both the suspected murder weapon and a tool he allegedly used to engrave the bullet cartridges. Robinson’s attorneys repeatedly questioned the reliability of DNA tests and other evidence from prosecutors.

President Donald Trump led reporters on a tour of the White House construction site on Tuesday, unveiling the new granite helipad on the South Lawn and holding forth at length on grades of stone, sightlines and square footage, five months into a war with Iran and days after asking the Supreme Court to let him resume work on a ballroom a federal appeals court ordered stopped.

The president summoned the White House press pool for the impromptu media availability to boast about the changes he has made to the Southern entrance to the building on Wednesday, during the time his public schedule had reserved for a “policy meeting.”

Instead of discussing policy with aides, he began to boast to the assembled cameras and journalists about the comparative attributes of granite versus asphalt for the White House driveway, wax about the living properties of grass and talk up his own prowess at renovation projects.

"I was very good at real estate, like maybe the best in a lot of ways, and I love construction," the president said. "I love seeing things properly taken care of."

Trump spent the bulk of the appearance on the stone itself. The white granite, which he said had been quarried in California, appeared to be cut in what he described as a radial pattern — "every stone is two degrees rounded," he said — and laid four inches thick, rather than the inch or inch and a half he said is standard. He returned repeatedly to its rated compressive strength of 35,000 pounds per square inch, against roughly 5,000 for hard concrete.

President Donald Trump speaks to the press at the construction site of a helipad on the South Lawn ( AFP/Getty )

"This granite has a million-year life," he said. "You'll never see a crack in this granite. I will go on the line. So in 10 years, if you see a crack, you'll say, 'Well, Trump just said you'll never see a crack.'"

He also said the helipad, which will bear a hand-carved seal, is "very close to being finished" and could be completed by the time Chinese president Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit next month.

While the president claimed that unnamed people had “wanted” a helipad at the White House for decades, the new project was made necessary by an unresolved problem with the next-generation helicopters slated for use as Marine One, the VH-92.

Manufactured by Sikorsky, the helicopters are far more powerful than the VH-3D Sea King aircraft that have ferried presidents to and from the South Lawn for decades, but that power comes with a downside: burnt grass.

After years of attempts to fix the problem, Sikorsky decided instead to pay for a helipad to eliminate the risk to grass from landing on the South Lawn.

The helipad is just one of numerous embellishments and changes the president has made to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue since returning to power last year, including his ongoing effort to replace the demolished East Wing with a massive ballroom that has been the subject of an ongoing court battle.

Trump described the ballroom now under construction as a joint project with the military, and disclosed a series of details about its design — a drone-proof roof, a fleet of drones stationed on top to defend Washington, a structure extending five stories and "almost 65 feet" underground, with shear walls of high-strength concrete.

"That structure is the most powerful because it's needed for bad purpose," he said, adding that it would withstand small-arms fire where the tents previously used for South Lawn events would not. "You take AK-47s. You take the most powerful. It laughs at it."

He then blamed a lawsuit for making those details public.

Trump attacked the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued over the project, calling it "a fake deal" and saying he had warned the organization that litigating would expose the building's security features.

"I said to them, you know, if you do this, you'll file it in court, and people will see what we're doing," he said. "And the enemy shouldn't be allowed to see it. They didn't care about that because they don't care about the country."

Asked what he would do if the Supreme Court ruled against him on the ballroom, Trump said he could not imagine it happening.

When Hayden Panettiere died this Sunday, the 36-year-old Heroes and Nashville star was in South Carolina with an on-and-off boyfriend she’d once described as her “abuser.”

Panettiere first started dating Brian Hickerson, an aspiring actor and real estate agent, in 2018. At the time, she had recently broken up with heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko, who is the father of her daughter, Kaya.

In the early days of their courtship, Panettiere and Hickerson were photographed by paparazzi in Los Angeles attending film screenings and eating brunch with friends.

However, by the following year their relationship had taken a dark turn. On May 2, 2019, according to Los Angeles County criminal court records, Hickerson was arrested on allegations of injuring a spouse or girlfriend. The alleged incident occurred at their home after a night of drinking, and Hickerson was subsequently ordered not to contact Panettiere and to stay at least 100 yards away from her.

That case was eventually dismissed, and the couple reunited only for another alleged violent incident to occur in Wyoming on Valentine’s Day 2020, when Hickerson was arrested once again. Later that year, prosecutors in Los Angeles charged him with four counts of injuring a spouse or cohabitant, two counts of assault with a deadly weapon, one count of dissuading a witness and one misdemeanor battery count, all linked to alleged incidents involving Panettiere between 2019 and 2020.

open image in gallery Hayden Panettiere and Brian Hickerson (pictured in 2019) started dating in 2018 ( Getty )

In July 2020, Panettiere spoke out about the way she had been treated. In a statement posted on Twitter (now X), she shared the number for a domestic abuse hotline online and wrote: “I am coming forward with the truth about what happened to me with the hope that my story will empower others in abusive relationships to get the help they need and deserve. I am prepared to do my part to make sure this man never hurts anyone again.”

Less than a year later, in April 2021, Hickerson pleaded no contest to two felony counts of injuring a spouse or girlfriend and was sentenced to 45 days in jail, four years of probation and 52 domestic violence classes.

However, the couple later rekindled their relationship once again. In April 2023, in the write-up of an interview with the New York Times, a journalist noted that Hickerson was “walking around, vacuuming and shooting a basketball through the hoop in her living area” during their meeting.

Panettiere admitted at the time that “there are feelings” between the pair, and that Hickerson had got sober and their relationship was “contingent on him continuing on this road of recovery.”

She added: “He knows he deserved what happened to him. I did not do any of this lightly.”

open image in gallery Panettiere was pronounced dead at a South Carolina apartment on August 16. The 911 call was made by Brian Hickerson ( Getty )

In May 2026, Panettiere, who was open about her own struggles with opioid addiction, published her memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning and reflected further on what her relationship with Hickerson had put her through.

She wrote that she never wanted to become a “spokesperson for domestic violence,” adding: “I never wanted to call myself a victim, but here I am. It’s part of my story whether I want it to be or not.”

In the book, Panettiere wrote that Hickerson beat her so badly on one occasion that she did not leave the house for weeks, and that she hesitated to report the alleged abuse to police out of concern that the public would find out.

When Panettiere was interviewed by The Independent that month, she said she was single. Her representatives stated that she and Hickerson were no longer in contact with one another, despite being photographed together a couple of months prior.

When Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, heard about her daughter’s death, she thought of Hickerson immediately. “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death and that was Brian Hickerson,” she told NBC News.

According to a police incident report, Brian and his brother Zach Hickerson called 911 when Panettiere was dying. Officers recorded that Zach was emotional as emergency services worked to save Panettiere’s life, but that Brian only became emotional after she was officially declared dead. The report also stated that Brian turned over a “bag of medication” belonging to Panettiere to investigators.

A cause of death has not been revealed, but an autopsy showed no signs of trauma.

In June, Panettiere shared a journal entry she had written reflecting on their relationship on Jay Shetty’s On Purpose podcast.

“I realized that I was more afraid of being alone than being abused,” she said. “In order to be around that behavior, it took me dulling my senses and numbing myself with substances in order to silence that rational voice in my head that was telling me exactly what was going on, and the many reasons why I needed to get myself out of this toxic relationship and as far away from this person as possible.”

Rape Crisis offers support for those affected by rape and sexual abuse. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk. If you are in the US, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673)

Potentially unsafe levels of fecal contamination have been detected in 85 percent of Missouri’s monitored recreational waterways, according to a report.​

The findings, which came just days after the Missouri Department of Natural Resources warned of high E.coli levels in Big River, have raised concerns about the safety of waterways in the state.

The analysis, published by Environment America Research & Policy Center last week, looked at findings from 202 monitoring locations placed at rivers, streams and lakes across Missouri.

A potentially unsafe level of fecal matter was found in 171 of those locations on at least one day in 2024 and 2025, the report reveals.

open image in gallery The ​Harry S. Truman Reservoir (pictured) was highlighted as an area with persistent bacterial risk ( Wiki Commons )

​​The agency warns that swimming, diving or even just wading in water contaminated with fecal bacteria can lead to skin, eye, ear and sinus infections, as well as gastrointestinal and respiratory illnesses.

“Having any degree of E.coli contamination or fecal contamination in our waters shouldn't be tolerated,” Abby Longo, who works with Environment America’s Safe for Swimming campaign, told KCUR.

“We ought to be entitled to swim and paddle in our waterways without being concerned about the consequences.”

The ​Harry S. Truman Reservoir, Grand Glaize Creek and Sycamore Creek were all highlighted as areas with persistent bacterial risk in 2024 and 2025, the report continued.

Data used by Environment America for the report was sourced from National Water Quality Monitoring Council’s Water Quality Portal.

​The findings were published days after the Missouri DNR confirmed in a press release that parts of Big River both upstream and downstream of the “failing” Leadwood wastewater treatment facility showed high levels of E.coli contamination.

The agency says that temporary repairs to the facility are being made while a lasting solution is found.

open image in gallery Environment America shared a map revealing the percentage of unsafe test days per water site. The key indicates how often the tests resulted in determinations that contamination levels were unsafe ( Environment America )

​E.coli and another microbe known as enterococci are used as indicator organisms to determine if fecal contamination has occurred, the Environmental Protection Agency says.

​In the report, Environment America says that polluted stormwater runoff, sewage overflows, livestock manure and failing septic systems can all be responsible for water becoming polluted.

​“Communities in Missouri could really reduce their sewage overflows and other sources of fecal bacteria,” Longo told KCUR. “But infrastructure projects like replacing sewer lines or upgrading wastewater treatment plants require pretty substantial resources.”

​For now, Longo says Missourians can apply for help through the Clean Water State Revolving Fund.

open image in gallery In addition to the ​Harry S. Truman Reservoir (pictured), Grand Glaize Creek and Sycamore Creek were also highlighted as areas with persistent bacterial risk in 2024 and 2025 ( Getty )

​However, in 2024, the EPA estimated that around $630 billion will be needed over 20 years in order to protect the U.S.’s waterbodies, following its report on wastewater, stormwater and clean water infrastructure needs.

​Environment America’s full report covered 17 states, including Alabama, New York, Pennsylvania and Michigan, among others.

The analysis found that contamination levels were potentially unsafe at 69 percent of locations in all 17 states for at least one day.

News.title: I’ve used the Google Pixel 11 Pro for a week, and I’m obsessed with this one feature
News.content:
Another year, another series of déjà vu-inducing Google Pixel phones. The Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold have just launched, but I wouldn’t say they’re filled with surprises.

I’ve spent the past week testing the Pixel 11 Pro, and well, it’s about what I expect from a Pixel phone. Everything is a little bit better than it was last year – the display is brighter, the cameras have been upgraded, the battery lasts longer and the processor is faster.

And while the camera bar has had a glow-up, with some flashy new HiLight LEDs and a thinner, edge-to-edge glass design, as always with a Pixel, it’s the software that steals the show. There are loads of new Gemini-powered tricks, but it’s one new camera feature in particular that has literally changed how I take photos. I’ve been putting the Pixel 11 Pro through its paces to see if it’s worth the upgrade.



open image in gallery ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

Google Pixel 11 Pro: Price and deals

The Google Pixel 11 Pro starts at £1,079 for the 256GB model. You can also get the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, which has a larger 6.8in display, starting from £1,279. To put that into context, the iPhone 17 Pro starts from £1,099 and the iPhone 17 Pro Max starts from £1,199, making the Pixel 11 Pro £20 cheaper than its Apple rival, but the larger Pro XL £80 more expensive.

That Google Pixel 11 Pro XL price could soon look a little less steep, however. The upcoming iPhone 18 Pro Max is heavily rumoured to get a price hike this year, with rising memory costs putting pressure on smartphone prices.

If you’re looking to bring the price down, Google is currently offering up to £850 off the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL when you buy directly from the Google Store. The deal runs until 1 September. You’ll get at least £400 off the new Pixel 11 Pro by trading in any phone, on top of the current valuation.

And to sweeten the deal even further, you can get up to £80 off a new Pixel Watch 5 until 1 September when you buy one with a Pixel 11 smartphone. This brings the 45mm Pixel Watch 5 LTE model down to just £419. You can also trade-in your current smartwatch to bring the price down even further.

Google Pixel 11 Pro: Design and display

open image in gallery LED lights around the flash glow when the phone is face down and Gemini is active ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

There’s something iconic about the Google Pixel – a big thumping camera bar on the rear; rounded corners; unmistakable Pixel colourways. You’ll know a Google Pixel phone when you see it.

The Pixel 11 Pro is almost a copy-paste of the Pixel 10 Pro, which itself looked like the Pixel 9 Pro. And that’s fine – it’s iconic for a reason. It’s still a handsome phone, with Gorilla Glass Victus 2 on the front and back, sandwiched around a polished aluminium frame.

What’s different about the design, however, is that the big camera bar has gone on a trip to the barber’s and asked for a shape-up, sides and back. The camera bar is 40 per cent thinner (and noticeably so). The black glass now stretches across its entire face, swallowing up the flash, which previously sat in its own little metal area. It protrudes a whole lot less and looks sleeker as one glass slab.

The most noticeable addition to the design is something called HiLight. Google’s put a ring of colourful LEDs around the camera flash. It lights up when the phone is face down, and looks like the entire flash is glowing. You can assign one of five different colours to contacts so you know who’s calling without picking up your phone. The lights also spring to life when Gemini is listening, thinking or responding. It looks almost like a waveform when Gemini is active and talking.

It’s basically Google’s take on Nothing’s Glyph Interface, except right now it can’t do anywhere near as much. At launch, HiLight can only light up for calls and Gemini, which is kind of... useless. Google says message notifications are coming later, but compare it to Nothing’s Glyph interface and it’s still nowhere near as good.

Nothing’s version can show you notifications from individual apps, keep important alerts permanently lit until you check them, act as a camera countdown and even show things like volume and charging progress. Are there really that many times you need a colourful light just to tell you who’s calling?

Like the Pixel 10 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro features a soft-touch matte glass back and polished aluminium frame, with a shiny reflective edge around the camera bar and Google logo. The colours are new, though, with canyon, olive, fog and obsidian. The new obsidian colourway also has an all-matte finish, with a matte Google logo and matte trim around the camera bar. I’ve been testing the fog model – it looks sleek with the polished accents.

Flip the Pixel 11 Pro over and you’ll find a nice 6.3in LTPO OLED Super Actua display. The size hasn’t changed, and neither has the adaptive 1Hz-120Hz refresh rate. Google has cranked the peak brightness up to 3,600 nits, which is 9 per cent brighter than last year. It’s sharp and wonderfully smooth to scroll on.

Google has also added a new coating to the Pro display that it says is twice as scratch resistant as before. I’m not about to start scraping a £1,079 review unit with my keys to find out, but one week in, my naked screen protector-free Pixel 11 Pro has no scuffs.

Google Pixel 11 Pro: Cameras

Google Pixel phones have always had some of the best cameras on any smartphone, and that’s still the case with the Pixel 11 Pro, despite not having many changes. Its triple-camera array features a 50MP main camera, 48MP ultrawide and 48MP 5x telephoto, plus a hefty 42MP selfie camera on the front.

The main snapper takes great photos, and while it’s not to everyone’s taste, I love Google’s saturation-heavy pics. They just make any photo pop, and always come out looking fantastic.

open image in gallery The main camera took bright and colourful pictures at Lord’s Cricket Ground ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

The biggest hardware upgrade this year is to that telephoto camera. Google has fitted it with a larger 1/2in sensor that captures 30 per cent more light than the Pixel 10 Pro. You can now also zoom all the way up to a frankly ridiculous 120x, up from 100x last year.

Sure, 120x sounds completely bonkers, but there is a catch. Once you zoom to 30x or beyond, Google uses an on-device generative AI model to reconstruct and sharpen details that the camera can’t capture on its own, so it’s not exactly a true 120x zoom. It saves that AI-enhanced image with a version without the generative processing, so you can compare the two and decide which one you prefer.

open image in gallery I performed a low-light photography zoom test ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

It’s also quicker to take photos at night, too. Instant Night Sight is essentially a much faster version of Google’s already excellent Night Sight. It uses the improved sensors and extra processing power to take faster low-light photos without making you stand completely still for what feels like an eternity. In my testing, it snapped photos in a second, rather than several seconds.

I took the same shot at 0.5x, 1x, 2x, 5x and 10x as the sun was going down, and the Pixel 11 Pro did a great job of keeping the bright sky under control and still pulling plenty of detail out of the brickwork. The 5x telephoto was particularly impressive, retaining loads of texture and detail despite the fading light.

There was an inevitable drop in sharpness once I pushed it to 10x, however, with the brickwork looking a little more processed. The picture was still decent, though, and colours and exposure were consistent.

While that’s all well and good, the camera feature that’s absolutely changed the way I take photos is the new Magic Capture feature. Rather than taking a single photo, one tap of the Magic Capture shutter starts capturing both video and high-quality stills. The Pixel then automatically pulls out some of the best shots and edits them so they look their best. The thing I love most, however, is that it solves one of the biggest gripes I have about taking photos.

If you’ve ever set a timer on a phone to try and get a group photo, you’ll know my pain. You rush into the frame, wait for a few seconds, rush back to see if it was any good, realise your pal had their eyes closed, then set another 10-second timer. Rinse and repeat.

Or maybe you’ve got a dog (or baby) who always looks away at the exact moment you hit the shutter button, ruining the picture you had spent minutes framing. Magic Capture fixes all of those annoyances. It’s genuinely made taking photos so much more hassle-free, and even saves the video, so you can pick your own frame if you prefer. Total gamechanger – in the settings, you can even set it so that the camera app always uses Magic Capture.

open image in gallery Not going to lie, I don't think I could take more accurate pictures than these ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

My social media editor Niki captured me spinning around in the office as one of my Magic Capture tests, and it captured some great stuff, with really decent image quality. It generally favours moments where the subject is looking towards the camera, giving me several different poses and expressions to choose from. It maintains the sharpness and detail in my face and clothes, despite me spinning quite fast. Exposure seems good too, especially with the bright windows and lights behind me.

It looks like a picture the Google Pixel would take even without Magic Capture turned on, with lots of colour and detail, and – crucially – they don’t look like random screenshots taken from a video.

Now, I can see why some people might not like it. You’re essentially giving away your photo-taking abilities to a robot. But as someone who – hands up – doesn’t care much for the integrity of their photography prowess, it’s the exact thing I’ve needed. My apologies to all the photography purists out there.

There’s also a new Camera Looks feature, which lets you give your photos a particular aesthetic before you’ve taken them. You can choose to highlight the shadows, pump up the warmer tones or choose different film styles. You can even adjust the amount of grain and set your favourite as the default every time you open the camera.

Unlike applying a filter on after you’ve taken a photo, Google says the Looks work directly within the camera’s imaging pipeline. I think the camera’s default settings are the best, so it’s not something I’ve found myself using very often.

In terms of video, the Pixel 11 Pro can now shoot 4K video in portrait, and there’s a new Pro Stable Video mode that uses something Google calls Video Boost to smooth out your footage when you’re moving around.

Google Pixel 11 Pro: Features and performance

As ever with a Pixel phone, though, the hardware isn’t why you buy one. Google has absolutely stuffed the Pixel 11 Pro with new software features, and while there’s the usual smattering of Gemini AI stuff I could probably live without, there are some features I’ve loved using.

The feature that has literally made me go “wow” is the new upgrade to Live Translate. It can now translate the actual audio from videos, podcasts and voice messages in real time. It essentially dubs whatever you’re listening to into another supported language. I tried this with a French language news service on YouTube and it kept the newsreader’s exact voice, but if they were speaking English instead of French. I can imagine this becoming so useful when watching a TV show that hasn’t yet been dubbed into English. It’s astonishing, and once Chinese is supported, I’m going to enjoy testing this out with the relatives I struggle to communicate with. It’s quite eerie seeing it work in real time as well.

It’s not perfect, however. I translated an interview with Timothee Chalamet talking French, and it got a few things wrong and went silent when it should’ve been translating. It’s cool, but it still needs a little work.

There’s also another neat new dictation feature. Rambler, which is powered by Gemini, lets you ramble your dictation instead of dictating every single word and punctuation. So you can talk naturally, and it’ll dictate what you actually want it to say. As a test, I dictated a shopping list text to a friend with lots of ums and pauses. I said things like “scrap that, we need milk instead of orange juice” and purposefully stumbled over my words. It fixed it all.

Now, I’m not a big fan of dictation generally, but for those who struggle with text, Rambler will have your messages typed out perfectly. I can picture it being a godsend for my mother, whose first language isn’t English and is always fretting about how her grammar or her word choice comes across over text.

You can correct yourself halfway through a sentence and Rambler will tidy everything up, stripping out the ums and ahs. It will also fix stutters, then add the correct punctuation where needed. Once you’ve finished, you can even carry on talking. It’ll edit what you’ve already written, so you can ask it to change a word, add something you forgot or rewrite the entire thing in a different tone of voice.

Circle to Search now works directly inside the camera as well, so you can point your Pixel at something and search for it or translate text without having to take a picture first.

Disappointingly, however, UK users don’t get Google’s new Proactive Assistance features at launch, which are the most powerful Gemini features on the Pixel 11. Active in other countries, it proactively surfaces useful information and actions based on what you’re doing on your phone, or what’s on the screen. Google showed how it can even react to your notifications and your location.

Google says those in the UK will get similar functionality through a feature called Magic Cue, but that’s not new – it debuted on the Pixel 10 last year. It’s not exactly the same.

As for performance, the Pixel 11 Pro is powered by Google’s new Tensor G6 processor and comes with 12GB of RAM on the 256GB model or 16GB on the 512GB and 1TB models. Google says the new chip makes web browsing 25 per cent faster and that apps launch 15 per cent quicker, with the phone using up to 20 per cent less power. I found that to be the case in my week with the Pixel 11 Pro. It’s never overheated when using RAM-intensive apps and games, and is buttery smooth to browse and scroll.

The Pixel 11 Pro launches with Android 17 and, as with recent Pixels, Google promises seven years of operating system, security and Pixel Drop updates. That means a Pixel 11 Pro bought today should still be receiving software updates in 2033.

Google Pixel 11 Pro: Battery life and charging

The battery life on the Pixel 11 Pro has also been improved. It now boasts a larger 4,850mAh battery, up from 4,700mAh on the Pixel 10 Pro. You get more than 30 hours on a single charge, up from the 24+ hours it promised with last year’s model. I found that to be broadly the case – in daily use, I could get it to last until the next morning. Heavier days of usage did require a plug in by the time I got to bed, however.

Charging has improved, too. The Pixel 11 Pro can reach 55 per cent charge in around 30 minutes with a 30W charger, although you’ll need to buy your own as there isn’t one in the box.

open image in gallery ( Alex Lee/The Independent )

The Pixel 11 Pro also supports even faster magnetic wireless charging. The Pixel 11 Pro now supports Pixelsnap charging at up to 25W, up from 15W on the Pixel 10 Pro. In my tests, it reached around 50 per cent in just 30 minutes, meaning wireless speeds are finally almost as good as wired speeds.

A neat new screensaver feature is also visible when the phone is charging. You can turn the display into a clock, show the weather or your Google Photos, or have it display detailed charging stats. It’s possible to set up several screensavers and swipe between them when the phone is docked on a Pixelsnap stand.

Key specifications:

Screen size: 6.3in

6.3in Resolution: 1,280 x 2,856 LTPO OLED, 1-120Hz

1,280 x 2,856 LTPO OLED, 1-120Hz Processor: Google Tensor G6

Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12GB/16GB

12GB/16GB Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB

256GB/512GB/1TB Rear cameras: 50MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP 5x telephoto

50MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP 5x telephoto Front camera: 42MP

42MP Battery: 4,850mAh

4,850mAh Charging: 30W wired, 25W Pixelsnap wireless

30W wired, 25W Pixelsnap wireless Operating system: Android 17

Android 17 Colours: Canyon, olive, fog, matte obsidian

Canyon, olive, fog, matte obsidian Water resistance: IP68

IP68 Dimensions: 152.8 x 72 x 8.5mm

152.8 x 72 x 8.5mm Weight: 204g

Should you buy the Google Pixel 11 Pro?

I hate to say it, but the Google Pixel 11 Pro is a fairly boring upgrade. Google hasn’t revolutionised smartphones, or anything like it. The design is largely the same, the display is only a little brighter and most of the camera hardware hasn’t changed. Even that new HiLight feature feels half-baked at launch.

But there’s no denying that Google is still hitting it out of the park when it comes to software. Live Translate genuinely blew me away, Rambler is a clever feature and Magic Capture has completely changed the way I take photos. These are all AI features that are actually improving those small daily annoyances, whether that’s with taking pictures, dictation or communication.

If you already own the Pixel 10 Pro, there probably isn’t enough here to justify spending £1,079 on an upgrade. But if you’re coming from an older Pixel or looking for one of the best Android phones you can buy, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great phone, though not quite remarkable.

How I tested the Google Pixel 11 Pro

I spent a week using the Google Pixel 11 Pro as my daily driver. I swapped to using Magic Capture for most of my photos, snapped pictures in daylight and after dark and tested the new 120x Pro Zoom. I streamed videos on YouTube and put Live Translate through its paces, tried out Rambler for dictation and used the phone for all my usual day-to-day tasks. I also tested battery life on lighter and heavier days and compared wired and Pixelsnap wireless charging speeds.

Every product is used as part of his everyday routine and judged on how it performs in daily life, helping readers find the gadgets that are worth buying.

News.title: Burnham blames Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation
News.content:
Andy Burnham has blamed Donald Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation in Britain.

Inflation jumped from 2.6pc in June to 2.9pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics, threatening to undermine Mr Burnham’s pledge to bring down the cost of living.

The Prime Minister said: “We can’t control though what is going on in the Middle East and the effect of the conflict there is now being felt in inflation here, and in other countries around the world.

“I realise these times are really hard but already people can see a month into office I have done things that will make a difference.”

July’s inflation figure was affected by a 13.5pc rise in the Ofgem price cap in response to the energy crisis unleashed by the Iran war. It means prices are now rising at their highest rate since March.

The latest figure shows the struggle that Mr Burnham faces to fulfil his promise to bring down living costs.

There are fears that inflation will climb higher in the coming months as the impact of the conflict filters through to the economy.

Speaking at an event in the North East, Mr Burnham added: “I want to lead a cost-of-living Government, and I’ve already taken steps as Prime Minister to show I will help people wherever I can. I can’t do everything, I think people know that.

“We’re in tough times, but where I can do something to make life that little bit better, I will do it.”

Since arriving in No 10, Mr Burnham has made tackling the cost of living a key policy focus.

The Prime Minister announced last month that he would remove VAT from electricity bills from October and reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares from next year.

However, average energy bills are expected to jump by around 4pc from October, according to energy analysts Cornwall Insight, wiping out any potential savings from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

The analysts said Ofgem’s price cap – which limits the average annual energy bill faced by a family home – would rise from £1,663 to £1,729.

Despite concerns about increasing gas and electricity bills, July’s rate of inflation was in line with economists’ expectations.

Money markets now expect policymakers at the Bank of England to hold interest rates at 3.75pc at their next meeting in September.

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

News.title: Top British scientist steps down from WHO
News.content:
One of Britain’s best-known scientists has resigned as assistant director-general of the World Health Organization.

Sir Jeremy Farrar became a household name during the pandemic when he served on the UK’s Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies (Sage).

Sources inside the WHO and the broader scientific community told The Telegraph he resigned his position on Monday.

While it is not clear what prompted his resignation, colleagues told The Telegraph he had been unhappy within the organisation for some time. One speculated that he had become increasingly frustrated with its internal politics and bureaucracy.

Sir Jeremy, 64, who was also a former director of the Wellcome Trust, could not immediately be reached for comment.

The surprise move comes at a difficult time for the WHO, which is undergoing a major restructuring after suffering cuts and a massive funding shortfall following the United States’s withdrawal from it in January. It is also fighting a major outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s Director-General, announced Dr Farrar’s decision in an email to all staff on Tuesday morning, saying that the British scientist will “retire” from the WHO, effective September 30.

In the email, seen by The Telegraph, Dr Tedros said: “Dr Farrar has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to science and public health at the highest levels, and we are grateful that he chose to bring his experience, energy and conviction to WHO.

“On behalf of the entire organisation, I extend my sincere thanks to Dr Farrar... [and wish] him every success in his next chapter and a well-deserved retirement.”

He added that Dr Bruce Aylward will take over as the new Assistant Director-General for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care.

Sports.title: Nicolas Jackson and Liam Delap among TWELVE players training away from Chelsea first-team with futures unclear
Sports.content:
LIAM DELAP and Nicolas Jackson are training separately from the main Chelsea squad with their futures unclear.

A group of up to 12 Blues players are working away from Xabi Alonso‘s main squad, either ahead of moves away or as they build up fitness.



Having been heavily criticised for their ‘bomb squad’ approach in recent seasons, which saw Raheem Sterling and Axel Disasi training alone last term, the club have changed things up this year.

Alonso insisted there would not be a repeat of the ‘bomb squad’ and, after consultation with the Professional Footballers’ Association last year and a period of what the club called self-reflection over the summer, a decision was made to change their approach.

Delap, Jackson and others in the group, which has also included new arrivals Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck as they work back to fitness, are training on first team pitches at the same time as Alonso’s squad. They are not, however, involved in the main session.

Last season Sterling posted to show he was training alone in the evening while, before joining West Ham on loan, Disasi would train at times with the academy.

Without European football this season, Chelsea know they need to reduce the size of their squad – with 41 players listed in the senior squad on the club’s website.

Chelsea currently have six strikers on their books but want to end with window with just three, meaning Jackson and Delap could both depart this summer.

EDERSON remains baffled as to why his Manchester United transfer collapsed, claiming his medical “went well”.

Dream Team is back, free, and there’s £100,000 up for grabs!

Meanwhile Ederson has since signed a new contract with Atalanta and spoke about his eventful summer ahead of the Italians’ Conference League play-off with Hapoel Tel-Aviv.

He said: “I honestly don’t know what happened. I always had interest from other clubs, and I could’ve gone to another English side.



“The tests went well, I don’t know what changed. I’ve been with Atalanta for four years and always played.

“I could’ve just waited to see what happened, but the great rapport with the club convinced me to stay and sign a new contract.”

Ederson had long been on United’s radar as they looked to replace fellow Brazil star Casemiro, who left for Inter Miami this summer.

Barcelona ready to pounce as Harry Kane makes contract stance clear to Bayern Munich

Harry Kane has entered the final year of his contract with Bayern Munich and the England captain is attracting interest from Barcelona in the summer transfer window

Barcelona are reportedly ready to move for Harry Kane if his contract talks with Bayern Munich don't go to plan. Kane has entered the final year of his deal with Bayern, who are aware of interest from elsewhere in the England captain.

Kane has scored a ludicrous 146 goals in 147 appearances since joining Bayern from Tottenham in a £86.4million deal in the summer of 2023. He is now 33 years old, but is showing no signs of slowing down as the most prolific goalscorer in Europe.

Bayern are ready to offer Kane fresh terms to keep him in Bavaria and the need for action is clear. The Daily Mail reports that Barca are monitoring the situation and have made their interest known.

‌



Kane is seeking a three-year deal to extend his stay in Germany and could use Barcelona's interest, and that of Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal, as a bargaining chip.

Barcelona have signed Anthony Gordon, Rodri and Karim Adeyemi so far this summer, but could do with another forward after selling Ferran Torres to Paris Saint-Germain and allowing Robert Lewandowski to leave upon the expiry of his contract. "We obviously said we wanted to talk after the World Cup and after my holiday," Kane said this week. "So I'm not sure exactly when, but they'll start this week, next week... we'll start those talks. Like I've said before, we're calm, I think they're calm with the situation.

"The Ballon d'Or is as big as it gets, from an individual point of view," he said. "I know I had a great season last season, but the focus is on this new season.

"The Ballon d'Or's not in my hands. I've done what I can do in terms of putting in the performances. It's now down to votes and other people and the media - stuff I can't control - so we'll see what happens.

"Obviously, it would be amazing if it was to happen. But ultimately, it's still two or three months away before that's decided so it's not something that's at the front of my mind right now."
